messages.subject: Goodness of fit statistics
messages.body_plain:
Hello blavaan community,

First-time poster, so first let me say thank you for such an excellent piece of software!

Are there ways to compute analogous fit statistics to those which are commonly reported in frequentist SEM, like CFI, RMSEA or Chi^2? I personally don't like to put much emphasis on fit statistics other than predictive validity, but I know that "traditional" SEM people (potential reviewers) might. Are BIC, DIC and WAIC the only options at my disposal if I use blavaan?

Reference: http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm

Thanks,
David

messages.subject: Re: Goodness of fit statistics
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

A metric somewhat similar to the chi-squared statistic is there, labeled as the posterior predictive p-value "ppp". Some further info on this is discussed in the appendix of the blavaan paper:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05604

The others (RMSEA, CFI, etc) are simple to compute, but I'm not quite sure what to do with them in a Bayesian context and have not seen them used there. So I probably won't add them until I see some more attention devoted to this issue (either from myself or from other researchers).

Ed

messages.subject: Using posteriors as priors
messages.body_plain:
Dear blavaan users,
I want to test the structural validity of a translated questionnaire with 37 items that, according to theory, load on three dimensions. The sample size is small (n=52). This is why I would like to use a Bayesian CFA.
Some properties of the original questionnaire have been already assessed with a similar sample size (n=44) and the authors sent me their database.
My question is: how can I use that data for my analysis?
I could run a Bayesian CFA with that database and use the posterior distributions as priors but I don't know how to include them in the model specification.
I could also extract some statistics (for example the means and sd of items) and specify the priors as described in the blavaan manual.

Thank you very much for any advice!

Best regards,
Mauro

messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
messages.body_plain:
> I could run a Bayesian CFA with that database and use the posterior distributions as priors

This should be mathematically equivalent to using a noninformative prior and fitting the model to all N = 52 + 44 = 96 observations.  So you could just combine the samples.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
messages.body_plain:
Mauro,

If you are seeing whether the current sample has similar properties to the previous sample, then you might also find a two-group model to be helpful. But you would probably also want to do a sensitivity analysis with the priors: at these sample sizes, I would guess that the priors of factor variances (and potentially other parameters) would have a sizable influence on the posterior.

Ed

Thanks Terrence Jorgensen and Ed Merkle for your answers.

My study goal is to assess some psychometric properties of a
self-report questionnaire that was translated from english language to
italian. The original version has been already assessed and the
results have been already published. However, the original authors did
not assess its structural validity, probably due to the small sample
size.
Even if I could merge the two samples (as suggested by Terrence
Jorgensen) or test the measurement invariance of the questionnaire (as
suggested by Ed Merkle), my first interest is to assess the structural
validity of the Italian language version by means of a Bayesian CFA.
Given that I have the dataset of the original study, I would like to
use it for specifying the priors of "my" parameters. Is this correct?
If it is, what is the procedure? Should I run a Bayesian CFA with the
original dataset and then use the posterior distributions that will
result as priors for my analysis?

Thank you very much!

Best regards,
Mauro

messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
messages.body_plain:
Mauro,

You could indeed run a cfa on the original data, then use those posteriors to define priors for your new data. One challenge here would involve defining distributions for the priors of your new model: the posteriors for the original data could give you a mean/sd for your priors, but those posteriors are not necessarily normal at n=44. Another challenge might involve prior sensitivity: the priors you use for the original data can influence the posteriors, which would then influence the prior for the new data.

Ed

messages.body_plain:
Dear Ed Merkle,
thank you very much for your answer!
With regard to the first challenge, I wondered if the posterior distributions could be used as they were in the analysis of my model but, if I have correctly understood your message, the only data that can be used are the parameters of the posteriors (for example, the estimated means and SDs). I thought that blavaan or JAGS or any other Bayesian software could use the whole posterior distributions.
Is there a way in blavaan to visualize the shapes of the posterior distributions and specify the priors accordingly? For example, if the posterior distribution of a factor loading is asymmetric, could I specify an asymmetric prior?
With regard to the second challenge, I could specify the priors for the original data as suggested in the paper titled "blavaan: Bayesian Structural Equation Models via Parameter Expansion", for example by placing uniform priors on the items' standard deviations with lower bounds at 0 and upper bounds at the maximum possible standard deviation (all items have a likert response scale with five levels: 0-1-2-3-4).
Do you think that following the example described in the paper could overcome the challenge?

Sincerely,
Mauro

messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
messages.body_plain:
Mauro,

The Bayesian software typically provides you with a full sample from each parameter's posterior distribution, but there are no guarantees that these distributions are normal or anything else. You could visualize the distributions with the plot function, something like

plot(fit, 1:4, "histogram")

where the "1:4" is for the first four model parameters.

Regarding the second challenge, uniform priors could be a good starting point, but the more general point is that the results may differ under other priors. You might try a sensitivity analysis using alternative sets of priors.

Ed

messages.subject: Survey design and blavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hello blavaan community,

I'm running a blavaan model on data from a stratified cluster survey, and I would like to adjust the point estimates and standard errors to account for survey design.

I'm aware of the survey  <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/survey/index.html>package and lavaan.survey  <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.survey/index.html>package, but I'm not sure how to implement them for a blavaan object.

Gelman 2013 "Bayesian Data Analysis 3rd Edition" (page 211) effectively recommends including a random effect at the cluster and stratum level, but I don't know how to do that either.

Any recommendations?

Thanks!
David

messages.subject: Re: Survey design and blavaan
messages.body_plain:
David,

I think this will take some work to automate in blavaan, and I doubt it will happen soon. For now, I think your best bet is to export a JAGS model without survey weights (using the jagfile=TRUE option in blavaan), then try to edit in the weights.

It might not be a terrible edit, because all the parameters in the JAGS file have a dimension for group indicator (the "g[i]"). I think you could use that indicator for your clusters, then assign a random effect to different levels of g[i]. But this would still require knowing your way around the JAGS code.

Ed

    y3[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i,6], 1/thetastar[6,6,g[i]])

model {
  for(k in 1:K) {
      for(j in 1:N[k]) {
        i = cs[k] + j
        x1[i] ~ dnorm(mu[k,1], 1/theta[1,1,g[k]])
        x2[i] ~ dnorm(mu[k,2], 1/theta[2,2,g[k]])
        x3[i] ~ dnorm(mu[k,3], 1/theta[3,3,g[k]])
        y1[i] ~ dnorm(mu[k,4], 1/thetastar[4,4,g[k]])
        y2[i] ~ dnorm(mu[k,5], 1/thetastar[5,5,g[k]])
        y3[i] ~ dnorm(mu[k,6], 1/thetastar[6,6,g[k]])

Where N is now a vector of length K, containing the cluster-level sample sizes, and cs is the cumulative sum of N (starting with 0 so that i still indexes observations, j indexes observations within clusters, and k indexes clusters).

Would this even work?

Thanks again,
David

> David,
>

I think that the "i = cs[k] + j" line would throw an error.

I would think to add an extra random effect to each mu, something like

mu[i,1] <- <the stuff already there> + cs[g[i],1]
mu[i,2] <- <the stuff already there> + cs[g[i],2]

Then, later in the code, there is an extra loop over clusters to define priors on the cs parameters. I vaguely remember Gelman's suggestion on this but haven't refreshed myself on the details, so I might be wrong.

Ed

messages.subject: Re: Using posteriors as priors
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ed,
thank you again for the advice.
I apologize for all the naive questions that I have submitted to you and the group. I am a beginner in the field of Bayesian analysis and I am quite disoriented about the use of previous knowledge in the analysis of new data.
I would have some other questions about the priors for factor variances and covariances but I don't want to bore you and the group.
Please let me know if I could write you again.

Thank you very much!

Sincerely,
Mauro

2017-01-24 19:20 GMT+01:00 Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com>:
> Mauro,
>
> The Bayesian software typically provides you with a full sample from each parameter's posterior distribution, but there are no guarantees that these distributions are normal or anything else. You could visualize the distributions with the plot function, something like
>
> plot(fit, 1:4, "histogram")
>
> where the "1:4" is for the first four model parameters.
>
> Regarding the second challenge, uniform priors could be a good starting point, but the more general point is that the results may differ under other priors. You might try a sensitivity analysis using alternative sets of priors.
>
> Ed
>
> On Tue, Jan 24, 2017 at 9:42 AM, Gian Mauro Manzoni <gianmaur...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Dear Ed Merkle,
> > thank you very much for your answer!
> > With regard to the first challenge, I wondered if the posterior distributions could be used as they were in the analysis of my model but, if I have correctly understood your message, the only data that can be used are the parameters of the posteriors (for example, the estimated means and SDs). I thought that blavaan or JAGS or any other Bayesian software could use the whole posterior distributions.
> > Is there a way in blavaan to visualize the shapes of the posterior distributions and specify the priors accordingly? For example, if the posterior distribution of a factor loading is asymmetric, could I specify an asymmetric prior?
> > With regard to the second challenge, I could specify the priors for the original data as suggested in the paper titled "blavaan: Bayesian Structural Equation Models via Parameter Expansion", for example by placing uniform priors on the items' standard deviations with lower bounds at 0 and upper bounds at the maximum possible standard deviation (all items have a likert response scale with five levels: 0-1-2-3-4).
> > Do you think that following the example described in the paper could overcome the challenge?
> >
> > Sincerely,
> > Mauro
> >
> >
> > 2017-01-24 15:32 GMT+01:00 Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com>:
> > > Mauro,
> > >
> > > You could indeed run a cfa on the original data, then use those posteriors to define priors for your new data. One challenge here would involve defining distributions for the priors of your new model: the posteriors for the original data could give you a mean/sd for your priors, but those posteriors are not necessarily normal at n=44. Another challenge might involve prior sensitivity: the priors you use for the original data can influence the posteriors, which would then influence the prior for the new data.
> > >
> > > Ed
> > >
> > >
> > > On Mon, Jan 23, 2017 at 12:34 PM, Gian Mauro Manzoni <gianmaur...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Thanks Terrence Jorgensen and Ed Merkle for your answers.
> > > >
> > > > My study goal is to assess some psychometric properties of a
> > > > self-report questionnaire that was translated from english language to
> > > > italian. The original version has been already assessed and the
> > > > results have been already published. However, the original authors did
> > > > not assess its structural validity, probably due to the small sample
> > > > size.
> > > > Even if I could merge the two samples (as suggested by Terrence
> > > > Jorgensen) or test the measurement invariance of the questionnaire (as
> > > > suggested by Ed Merkle), my first interest is to assess the structural
> > > > validity of the Italian language version by means of a Bayesian CFA.
> > > > Given that I have the dataset of the original study, I would like to
> > > > use it for specifying the priors of "my" parameters. Is this correct?
> > > > If it is, what is the procedure? Should I run a Bayesian CFA with the
> > > > original dataset and then use the posterior distributions that will
> > > > result as priors for my analysis?
> > > >
> > > > Thank you very much!
> > > >
> > > > Best regards,
> > > > Mauro
> > > >
> > > > 2017-01-23 17:50 GMT+01:00 Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com>:
> > > > > Mauro,
> > > > >
> > > > > If you are seeing whether the current sample has similar properties to the
> > > > > previous sample, then you might also find a two-group model to be helpful.
> > > > > But you would probably also want to do a sensitivity analysis with the
> > > > > priors: at these sample sizes, I would guess that the priors of factor
> > > > > variances (and potentially other parameters) would have a sizable influence
> > > > > on the posterior.
> > > > >
> > > > > Ed
